candidates.attacker_control: The `job` argument of the Pipeline `build` step is stored by BuildTriggerStep and may be an absolute or relative job path; the parameters, wait, and quietPeriod values are also controlled by the Pipeline author or caller. The target can therefore be a job outside the caller's permitted scope.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The only permission check in the repository is in doAutoCompleteJob (Item.READ), which is a UI autocomplete path and does not protect execution. No ACL or permission checks appear in BuildTriggerStepExecution, BuildTriggerListener, BuildQueueListener, or BuildTriggerAction. I also considered descriptor job/parameter checks, reflection used to read quietPeriod, and queue-action folding; none establishes authorization for scheduling. The snapshot does not include Jenkins core, so I could not inspect whether getItem or schedule2 independently enforce permissions.
candidates.impact: Authorization bypass: a user may start builds of jobs they are not permitted to build, potentially causing security-sensitive downstream deployment/release jobs to execute, consuming build resources, and queueing work under an upstream cause. When wait is enabled, the step also observes the downstream build result.
candidates.prerequisites: The attacker can cause a Pipeline containing the `build` step to execute under an identity that lacks Job/Build on the named target. The target must exist as a queue-task item and its name must be known or guessable, which is typical for a Pipeline author who is not authorized to build a protected downstream job.
candidates.root_cause: BuildTriggerStepExecution.start resolves the target from the user-controlled `job` string and immediately schedules it via ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2 or Queue.schedule2. Neither branch checks that the Pipeline's authentication has Item.BUILD on the target; no ACL, hasPermission, or checkPermission call is present in the execution path. Contextual name resolution only locates the item and does not establish authorization.
candidates.title: Pipeline build step triggers downstream jobs without Job/Build authorization
candidates.trace: BuildTriggerStep(String job) stores the untrusted name -> BuildTriggerStepExecution.start() calls Jenkins.getActiveInstance().getItem(job, invokingRun.getParent(), Item.class) -> the parameterized-job branch at lines 70-97 invokes scheduleBuild2, or the generic Queue.Task branch at lines 101-134 invokes Queue.schedule2 -> no item.hasPermission(Item.BUILD) check occurs before either scheduling call.
candidates.unverified: Runtime was not executed. Jenkins core and plugin dependency sources are outside the snapshot, so the candidate relies on the expected behavior that getItem performs name resolution and that scheduleBuild2/schedule2 are scheduling primitives without an Item.BUILD check. The exact authentication principal used by the Pipeline execution is also not observable here. This is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

coverage_summary: The source scope contains 13 files: one POM, one gitignore, six Java source files, and five resources. I listed all 13, directly read the POM, gitignore, six Java files, and Messages.properties, and inspected the four small HTML help resources through text-search results because direct reads failed with a path-encoding error. I reviewed the step's input handling, job resolution, scheduling, parameter completion, queue/build action lifecycle, listeners, cancellation, and UI descriptor endpoints. No test sources or dependency source trees are included.
limitations: Jenkins core and dependency sources are not part of the snapshot, so getItem, ParameterizedJobMixIn.scheduleBuild2, and Queue.schedule2 semantics could not be inspected directly.
No runtime execution, tests, or scanners were used; the candidate is not runtime-confirmed.
The four resource HTML files could not be read directly due to a repository path-encoding/tool error; their relevant text was inspected through search results.
Authorization policy and ACL configuration are outside this source snapshot, so the executing Pipeline's exact authentication principal is unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: BuildTriggerStep.DescriptorImpl.doCheckJob resolves an item and reports whether it is a supported Queue.Task without checking Item.READ (BuildTriggerStep.java lines 216-230).
rejected_leads.reason: This may allow limited disclosure of a hidden job's existence or item type through a UI validation endpoint, but the impact is information disclosure rather than execution of a protected operation, and no sensitive data return is shown. It was not selected as the strongest issue.

rejected_leads.lead: doAutoCompleteJob's relative-name traversal and ../ handling (BuildTriggerStep.java lines 132-185).
rejected_leads.reason: The traversal has explicit Item.READ checks for candidate items and only returns names of Queue.Tasks; I found no concrete unauthorized sensitive operation. Potential exceptions from unusual container paths are robustness concerns, not the strongest security finding.

rejected_leads.lead: Reflection used to invoke getQuietPeriod on arbitrary Queue.Tasks (BuildTriggerStepExecution.java lines 115-126).
rejected_leads.reason: It only invokes a public no-argument getter on an already-resolved item and catches reflection failures; no attacker-controlled class loading or invocation target was found. Queue-action synchronization and foldIntoExisting were also reviewed and did not yield a distinct security issue.

summary: The strongest source-supported lead is an authorization gap in the Pipeline `build` step: the execution resolves a user-supplied target job and schedules it without checking `Item.BUILD` for that target. The repository's only permission check is in a UI autocomplete path, so a Pipeline running with an identity that lacks build permission on a protected downstream job appears able to trigger that job anyway.
